$comment: Documentation navigation. Hand-maintained: the wiki has no ordering of its own, so this file is the single source of truth for sidebar structure, short nav labels and search-engine descriptions. `kind: "guide"` resolves to content/docs/<slug>.md, which the wiki sync owns; adding `"source": "authored"` reads content/guides/<slug>.md instead, which is authored in this repository and never touched by the sync. `kind: "page"` is a route implemented in src/app.

pages.title: OPEN//77 documentation
pages.description: How OPEN//77 packages gameplay as resources: the session model, the authoritative server, a hello-world manifest, and the conventions shared by every Lua API.

pages.title: How OPEN//77 works
pages.description: What OPEN//77 is and is not, how players connect, why it is built on dedicated servers rather than peer-to-peer sessions, the project roadmap, and answers to the questions people ask most.

pages.title: Host your own server
pages.description: A step-by-step guide to running your own OPEN//77 dedicated server: get the Windows or Linux build, mint a license key, walk the first-run setup, edit server.jsonc, launch it, and watch it appear automatically in the launcher.

pages.title: Server licensing
pages.description: How a server joins the OPEN//77 platform: create an account, mint a license key in the keymaster, put the key in your server config, and how the master authorises the server on boot.

pages.title: Warden
pages.description: Warden is the OPEN//77 in-server admin panel: a browser control room for your live server. Stream the console, run commands, hot-reload Lua resources, moderate players, post announcements, edit config and manage admins — without ever restarting.
Resource manifests, the client and server runtime split, signing and download, hot reload, and the security model around resources the server hands to connecting players.

pages.title: The Lua resource runtime
pages.description: What a resource actually gets: the complete manifest reference, the scheduler and lifecycle events, local and network events, modules and cross-resource exports, the core Open77 namespaces, WebUI surfaces, and every sandbox quota.
Durable player identifiers, session-scoped ids, display names, the rename flow, and what a game server can actually verify about a connecting player.
Exporting a public identity, whitelisting a player, and declaring restricted server commands behind the access control list.

Every dedicated-server global, Open77 namespace, permission, constant and result shape: scheduler, events, commands, players, combat, routing buckets, loot, vehicles, NPCs, elevators, database and logging.

pages.title: The join-time readiness gate
pages.description: Open77.ready: the host-owned barrier that stops one resource teleporting, spawning or killing a player another resource is not finished with. Holds, timeouts, the session number, and the rule every gamemode must follow.

pages.title: Operator tunables
pages.description: Open77.tunables: declaring the numbers a server owner may retune live from the admin panel, the file-scope local that silently defeats it, and choosing between live, promote and per-match capture.
Every client export published by the official OPEN//77 resource packages, with signatures per package and how to call them safely across resources.
Network vehicle identity, streaming, authority leases, seats and proxy replication, doors and glass, damage profiles, and the full asymmetric server and client Lua API.
Server-owned NPCs: templates, streaming, authority leases, the task queue, health and damage, events, the read-only client API, and the current limitations.
Server-authoritative native lifts: adopting a LiftDevice, bucket and chunk streaming, movement and pause control, late-join catch-up, and the reference resource commands.
Authoritative ground drops: creating and projecting item drops, validating pickups, the onLootPickup hook, and where native UI ends and server authority begins.
Synchronised session time and weather: the network model, shared configuration, ACL-gated commands, random weather events, and the server and client APIs.

pages.title: Drawing in the world
pages.description: Every way a Lua resource puts something at a point in Night City: native ground markers, per-frame world anchors and the native card, ring and dot overlays, the marker-plus-prompt POI facade, proximity zones and nameplates — with lifecycle and cleanup for each.
Vanilla map markers and mappins: creating and updating blips, attaching them to entities, custom icon metadata, stable aliases, and the complete sprite catalogue.
Custom world and NPC prompts: attaching interactions to players or NPCs, multiple actions and hold keys, the definition reference, and keeping server authority intact.
The open77_worldui facade: a ground marker and its interaction prompt created and destroyed as one owned handle, the definition reference, and the invisible-ring trap it exists to avoid.
The open77_zones service: enter and exit events with hysteresis, the definition reference, the polling model and quotas, and why every containment rule must still be re-derived on the server.
Reusable WebUI toasts: local client notifications, server-targeted delivery, updating and dismissing, queue limits, positions and progress.
Resource-owned world and entity visual effects plus spatialised sound effects, with inspection, cleanup and the curated alias catalogues.
Chat messages, slash commands, completion, and the built-in developer commands available to every player.
The write-only client clipboard API, the clipboard.write permission, failure reasons, and the built-in /pos and /rot transform commands.
Endpoint- and resource-isolated local key/value persistence: CRUD, search, atomic operations, quotas, and why it must never hold secrets.

pages.title: Writing a gamemode
pages.description: The shape of an OPEN//77 gamemode: why the server is exactly one resource and the client is several, the platform behaviours that bite every author, moving players safely, isolating a round in a routing bucket, and what to test first.
Why there is no shared server-side gamemode resource on OPEN//77, what a mode's server gets instead, and the eight conventions two shipped gamemodes both implement.

pages.title: Lua API reference
pages.description: Searchable reference for every registered OPEN//77 Lua function, separated by runtime so a client projection is never mistaken for server authority.
NPC templates, vehicle records, seat and door constants, items, weapons, effects, sounds, animations and sprite catalogues, with explicit support levels.
The ACL-gated in-game Lua laboratory: client execution, native lab commands, the REDscript bridge, and the limits that keep it out of gameplay code.

The MCP server and Claude Code skill that let an AI agent test OPEN//77 in the running game: the tool list, the human-path connection, repeatable scenarios, installation, and the rules that keep a verdict honest.
